## Overview

`add("2", "3")` returns the string `"23"`, not `5`. The function does no numeric coercion.

## How it works

`calc.js` is three lines and holds one function.

```js
export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

The single `+` operator decides its behavior from the operand types at runtime. JavaScript reaches for numeric addition only when both operands are numbers, primitives it can coerce to numbers (booleans, `null`), or a mix of number and numeric string. Two strings match the string-concatenation case first, so `+` joins them instead of summing them. `add("2", 3)` also concatenates to `"23"`, because one string operand is enough to select the string path.

Evidence from running the module under Node v24.21.0 with `node --input-type=module -e "await import('file://<work>/calc.js')"`.

| Call | Result | Type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `add("2", "3")` | `"23"` | string |
| `add(2, 3)` | `5` | number |
| `add("2", 3)` | `"23"` | string |
| `add([1], [2])` | `"12"` | string |

## Where things live

`calc.js` in the work tree is the whole module. It exports one function and imports nothing. Git history holds a single commit for the file, `e21f4e6 calc`.

## Gotchas

The function trusts its inputs completely. It has no guard, no `Number()` coercion, and no `typeof` check, so a caller passing form values or CLI arguments gets a silent concatenation rather than an error. That matters because the strings a caller is most likely to pass come from exactly those sources. If a caller wants addition, it converts at its own boundary, or `add` gains a parsed numeric contract.

Two side effects of the same mechanism are worth knowing. TypeScript would reject `add("2", "3")` at compile time given an `(a: number, b: number)` signature, so this bug shows up in untyped or `any`-typed call paths. And since `+` is also the array-to-string operator, an array argument concatenates instead of throwing.

No files were changed. `git status` is clean.
